documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
64M here to establish. Self-employed handyman (carpentry, small repairs, some roofing), lives alone in Granby, divorced. Previous PCP office he describes as hard to reach.

PMH
- HTN, on lisinopril 20 for about 8 years. Home cuff log he brought is at goal.
- Duodenal ulcer 2015: had black stools, scoped at his old practice, ulcer in the duodenum, H. pylori positive, treated, did a course of acid blocker afterward and stopped it. Nothing since.
- Neck: stiff for years, worse turning to back out of a driveway. Was told the neck films showed arthritis/disc wear. No arm symptoms.
No surgeries. NKDA.

Meds: lisinopril 20 daily, aspirin 81 daily, atorvastatin 40 daily. Aspirin and statin were started by the old PCP for prevention given BP, smoking history and his father's heart attack. He has no cholesterol diagnosis he knows of.

FH: father MI at 58. Mother arthritis. Brother has high blood pressure.
SH: smoked about a pack a day for 20 years, quit 2014. 1-2 drinks a month. No drugs.

ROS: no chest pain, no exertional breathlessness, no leg swelling, no melena since 2015, no reflux symptoms.

Exam: well-appearing, vitals as charted. HEENT normal. Neck: rotation mildly limited both ways, no tenderness. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft, nontender. No edema. Neuro: strength and reflexes symmetric in the arms.

A/P
1. Hypertension, at goal on lisinopril 20. Continue.
2. Prevention: aspirin and atorvastatin continue for now; lipids today.
3. History of duodenal ulcer, quiet for 4 years. If he ever needs an anti-inflammatory he is to call first.
4. Cervical spondylosis, mechanical, stable.
5. Health maintenance: Tdap today. CBC, CMP, lipids, A1c, TSH, one-time HCV and HIV screens. He qualifies for lung screening (20 pk-yr, quit 5 yr ago) and wants it: LDCT ordered. Colonoscopy 2017 per his report, getting the record. Flu shot when the vaccine arrives next month.
RTC 5-6 months.

- 2016: cervical spine x-rays for neck stiffness: multilevel disc space narrowing and facet degenerative change, no fracture or listhesis.
- 2017: screening colonoscopy, complete exam, no polyps or other findings; 10-year interval recommended.
- Hypertension managed on lisinopril 20 mg; aspirin 81 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg on the list.
- Allergies: none recorded.
Abstracted by MA; PCP reviewed.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: shoulders and elbows.
HPI: 67M, handyman. Says both shoulders and both elbows have been aching more and more for about two years. It builds over the workday and is worst in the evening after a day of overhead work or running a drill; rest takes the edge off. In the morning he is stiff for only a few minutes and then loosens up. No fevers, rashes, weight loss, recent illness. Never injured these joints. No history of inflammatory arthritis that he knows of. Neck is his usual neck.
Exam: vitals as charted. Shoulders and elbows: crepitus with passive range of motion bilaterally. No warmth, no effusion or real swelling. ROM modestly limited at the end ranges by pain. Strength full and symmetric. Sensation intact in both arms. No nodules, no skin changes over the joints.
Assessment: degenerative arthritis of shoulders and elbows, fits with decades of manual work; picture is mechanical, not inflammatory. Neck spondylosis known.
Plan: ESR and CRP to be thorough. Wants something he can take on heavy days. Indomethacin 25 mg up to three times daily as needed with food. Given the old duodenal ulcer and daily aspirin, adding pantoprazole 40 mg daily alongside it. Ice/heat, pacing overhead work. Call if black stools or stomach pain.

documents.title: Inflammation markers
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Alan, the two inflammation tests (sed rate 12 and CRP 2) are normal, which fits wear-and-tear arthritis rather than an inflammatory type. Keep the indomethacin to the days you need it and take the pantoprazole every day.

documents.author: PCP

S: About 3 weeks of getting more short of breath with exertion, fatigue, and a cough that comes on at night lying down. Both ankles swell by evening. No chest pain he will admit to, no fever, no sputum. Weight up about 3 kg since summer per our scale.
O: Vitals as charted. Mildly winded walking from the lobby. JVP hard to see with his neck. Heart regular. Lungs: crackles at both bases. Ankles: pitting edema bilaterally.
A: New exertional dyspnea, orthopneic cough and edema in a 67-year-old ex-smoker with HTN and a strong family history. Heart failure is the main concern.
P: BMP and CBC today. Called the cardiology office directly and got him in on 12/7 for consultation and echocardiogram. Precautions reviewed: 911 for chest pain or breathlessness at rest.

conditions.label: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

medications.drug: 24 HR metoprolol succinate 50 MG Extended Release Oral Tablet

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every morning

reports.text: Left ventricle is dilated. The anterior wall is thinned and dyskinetic, consistent with a left ventricular aneurysm. Remaining segments contract. Visually estimated LVEF 35%. Mitral valve leaflets structurally normal with a central regurgitant jet, functional mitral regurgitation, moderate. Aortic valve trileaflet without stenosis. Right ventricle normal in size and function. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Dilated LV with anterior wall dyskinesis (aneurysm); LVEF 35%. Moderate functional mitral regurgitation.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm. Deep Q waves across the anterior precordial leads with persistent ST-segment elevation in the same leads. No acute changes elsewhere.
reports.conclusion: Anterior Q waves with persistent ST elevation, consistent with old anterior infarct and aneurysm.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group, consultation letter to referring PCP.

Reason: worsening breathlessness and fatigue with a nocturnal cough and leg swelling.

History: 67-year-old self-employed handyman, hypertensive, former smoker (20 pack-years), father with MI at 58. Over recent weeks he has become progressively more winded and tired, and coughs mostly at night. Legs swell. He recalls no episode of crushing chest pain.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, indomethacin 25 mg as needed. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 130/85, HR 88, RR 18. Holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating toward the axilla. Bibasilar crackles. 2+ pitting edema of both legs.

Studies today: echo shows a dilated LV with a dyskinetic anterior wall and LVEF about 35%, with moderate functional MR. ECG: deep anterior Q waves with ST elevation that persists, the pattern of an established anterior aneurysm rather than an acute event.

Impression:
1. Ischemic cardiomyopathy: prior unrecognized anterior MI with LV aneurysm; heart failure with reduced EF, volume overloaded.
2. Coronary artery disease, presumed LAD territory.
3. Hypertension.

Plan: start metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and furosemide 40 mg each morning. Continue lisinopril 20, aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40. Daily weights; call for a gain over 1 kg in a day or 2 kg in a week. BMP in one week. Coronary angiography to be scheduled. Thank you for the referral.

Allergies: NKDA.

documents.title: Results and check-in
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt with BMP: kidney function and potassium fine on the new furosemide. He says he is peeing a lot in the morning and the ankles are already down. Home scale down about 3 kg. Coughing less at night. Reviewed daily weights and the cardiology call parameters. Cath date pending from cardiology. Copy of cardiology letter in chart.

medications.sig: Place 1 tablet under the tongue every 5 minutes as needed for chest pain, up to 3 doses; call 911 if not relieved

reports.text: Access: right radial artery. Left main: normal. Left anterior descending: severe 90% stenosis in the proximal segment, distal vessel fills normally. Left circumflex: no significant stenosis. Right coronary artery: no significant stenosis. Intervention: proximal LAD lesion predilated and treated with a single paclitaxel-coated drug-eluting stent, postdilated. 0% residual stenosis, TIMI 3 flow, no dissection. Radial band applied, hemostasis achieved.
reports.conclusion: Single-vessel CAD: severe proximal LAD stenosis treated with a paclitaxel-coated drug-eluting stent. Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm. Anterior Q waves with persistent ST elevation, unchanged from 12/2022. No new ST changes.

documents.body: Regional hospital ED. 67M with recently diagnosed ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 35%, anterior aneurysm), awaiting outpatient cath, woke at 0400 with central chest pressure at rest lasting about 20 minutes, a second shorter episode in the car. Pain free on arrival. ECG with the known anterior Q waves and ST elevation, unchanged from the cardiology tracing in December. First troponin normal. Cardiology aware; admitted to the cardiac unit for unstable angina and catheterization. Allergies: NKDA.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Admitted 1/11/2023, discharged 1/13/2023.
Diagnosis: unstable angina; single-vessel coronary disease; ischemic cardiomyopathy with LV aneurysm, HFrEF.
Course: rest angina, troponin normal on serial testing, ECG unchanged. Catheterization 1/12 via right radial: severe proximal LAD stenosis, treated with one paclitaxel-coated drug-eluting stent with an excellent result; other vessels without significant disease. No further chest pain. Radial site clean.
Discharge medications: aspirin 81 mg daily; clopidogrel 75 mg daily (new, do not stop without talking to cardiology); metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily; lisinopril 20 mg daily; furosemide 40 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily; pantoprazole 40 mg daily; nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL as needed (new); indomethacin 25 mg as needed per home list.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week; cardiology in about 6 weeks.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 6 days after discharge. Stent to proximal LAD 1/12 for rest angina. No chest pain since. Breathing better than before Christmas; sleeping on one pillow. Right wrist bruised, healing. Asking when he can get back on a ladder.
Meds reconciled with discharge list: aspirin, clopidogrel (new), metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40, SL NTG (new). Indomethacin as needed per list.
Exam: vitals as charted, weight down from December. Heart regular, apical systolic murmur. Lungs clear. Trace ankle edema. Radial site without hematoma.
A/P: CAD s/p PCI, HFrEF, euvolemic-ish. Continue DAPT without interruption. Light work only for a week, no heavy lifting from the right arm for a few more days. Keep daily weights. Cardiology f/u end of February is booked.

Follow-up letter. Mr. Babcock is about six weeks out from a drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD, placed in January for unstable angina, on a background of coronary disease, HFrEF and an anterior LV aneurysm. Since then he has had no chest pain and no breathlessness. He takes aspirin and clopidogrel every day without missed doses. Blood pressure and heart rate are well controlled on today's readings. For the record, the stent from the January procedure is a paclitaxel-coated device.

Medications: aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40, nitroglycerin SL as needed, indomethacin 25 as needed. NKDA.

Plan: continue current regimen including dual antiplatelet therapy. Return in about 2 months with a repeat echo.

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department.
CC: chest pain with breathing, fevers.
HPI: 67M with CAD and LV aneurysm, about ten weeks after LAD stent, reports two weeks of sharp chest pain that catches when he takes a deep breath and eases when he sits up and leans forward. Low-grade temperatures at home. Not like his January pressure.
Meds per patient: aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, lisinopril, furosemide, atorvastatin, pantoprazole, indomethacin as needed. NKDA.
Exam: vitals stable, hemodynamically sound. Friction rub heard at the left sternal border. Lungs clear. No JVD.
Data: WBC 12.0, Hgb 14.2, ESR 55, CRP 25 mg/L, troponin I <0.04 ng/mL. ECG diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Bedside echo: small effusion, no tamponade.
Impression: post-MI pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).
Plan: colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 3 months; aspirin 650 mg three times daily for 2 weeks then back to 81 mg; continue clopidogrel. Discharged home. Cardiology aware, PCP follow-up within a week. Return for worsening pain, breathlessness or lightheadedness.

documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED.
CC: neck pain, both hands weak after car accident.
HPI: 68-year-old man, known cervical spondylosis and coronary disease, was the driver of a pickup struck from behind while stopped at a light this afternoon. Belted. Immediate neck pain; since then both hands feel weak and clumsy and numb. Did not pass out. Legs feel normal.
Meds: aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril, furosemide, atorvastatin, pantoprazole, indomethacin as needed, SL nitroglycerin as needed. NKDA.
Exam: c-collar in place on arrival. Neck range limited by pain. Grip weak bilaterally, fine finger movements slow and clumsy. Light touch and pinprick reduced in both arms, most in the hands. Biceps and brachioradialis reflexes diminished both sides; knee and ankle reflexes normal. Lower extremity strength full. No incontinence; rectal tone intact.
MRI cervical spine: no fracture, chronic degenerative changes.
Plan: spine surgery consulted; observation overnight with neuro checks.

documents.title: Spine Surgery Consultation
documents.author: spine surgery
documents.body: Asked to see for bilateral hand weakness and sensory change after a rear-end collision on a background of cervical degenerative disease. Exam as documented by ED; lower extremities intact. MRI shows no fracture and chronic degenerative change only. No instability. Recommend nonoperative care: soft collar for comfort for 2 weeks, outpatient physical therapy, neuro checks overnight. No surgical intervention indicated. Return precautions for leg weakness, gait change, bowel or bladder change.

documents.title: Observation Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
Observation 3/1 to 3/2/2024.
Reason: neck injury in a rear-end collision with bilateral hand weakness and sensory change.
Course: neuro checks stable overnight. Hand strength slightly better this morning. Burning, pins-and-needles pain in both hands keeps him up. Spine surgery: nonoperative.
Discharge diagnosis: neuropathic pain syndrome of both upper extremities after neck injury, on cervical spondylosis. No fracture.
New medication: gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime.
Continue home medications unchanged. NKDA.
Orders: soft collar as needed; outpatient PT referral to be placed by PCP.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week.

orders.reason: hand weakness and neck pain after collision, cervical spondylosis

documents.title: Post-Observation Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Rear-ended last Friday, overnight observation, MRI without fracture. Hands: grip is coming back slowly, still dropping screws. Burning and tingling in both hands, worst at night; gabapentin at bedtime helps him sleep. Neck sore. Legs fine, walking fine, no bladder issues.
Exam: neck tender paraspinal, rotation limited. Grip reduced bilaterally, better than the ED described. Light touch reduced in the fingertips both hands. Biceps and brachioradialis reflexes still diminished. Gait normal.
A/P: neuropathic pain in both hands after neck injury on spondylosis, improving motor. PT referral placed. Continue gabapentin 300 at bedtime for now. No driving until he can turn his head and grip the wheel well. Recheck 4 weeks.

documents.title: Physical Therapy Initial Evaluation
documents.author: physical therapy
documents.body:
Outpatient PT evaluation. 68M, self-employed handyman, 11 days after a rear-end collision with neck pain and bilateral hand weakness and sensory change; cervical spondylosis; nonoperative per spine surgery. Goals: return to using hand tools, fasteners, driving.
Findings: cervical rotation limited and painful; grip and pinch reduced bilaterally; fine motor (coin pickup, buttoning) slowed; sensation diminished in the fingertips; gait and balance normal.
Plan: twice weekly for 8 weeks: cervical mobility, postural work, graded grip and dexterity training, home program. Cardiac precautions noted (HFrEF, CAD).

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule by mouth three times daily

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Four weeks out. PT twice a week, likes it. Grip clearly stronger, can run a screwdriver again but tires quickly. The burning in both hands persists through the day now, not just at night. Gabapentin at bedtime tolerated, no fogginess.
Exam: grip improved bilaterally. Fingertip light touch still reduced. Neck rotation better.
A/P: neuropathic pain syndrome, hands; motor recovering. Gabapentin increased to 300 mg three times daily. Kidney function normal on last labs. Caution re drowsiness on ladders. Continue PT. Back to driving short trips is reasonable now.

documents.title: Physical Therapy Discharge Summary
documents.author: physical therapy
documents.body: Discharged from PT after 15 visits (one missed). Cervical rotation now functional both directions. Grip and pinch close to expected for age and work; dexterity tasks within normal time. Residual intermittent burning in the fingertips, managed by his physician. Independent with home exercise program.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm. Anterior Q waves with persistent ST elevation, unchanged from prior tracings.

documents.title: Cardiology Annual Follow-up
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Letter to PCP. Seen for yearly review of CAD (proximal LAD DES 1/2023), ischemic cardiomyopathy with anterior aneurysm and HFrEF. No angina. Stable class II symptoms. Car accident in March with hand symptoms, now on gabapentin. ECG unchanged. Euvolemic on exam.
Medications: aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40, gabapentin 300 TID, indomethacin as needed, NTG SL as needed. NKDA.
Plan: continue current therapy including dual antiplatelet therapy. Return in one year.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV, age 69. Grip back to where it was before the accident since about June, back to small carpentry jobs. Fingertip burning still there most days but milder on gabapentin 300 TID. Neck stiff as always. Heart: stairs with mild breathlessness, unchanged. Saw cardiology in June, no changes.
No falls. PHQ-2 negative. Lives alone, independent.
Exam: vitals as charted. Grip strong and symmetric. Fingertip light touch mildly reduced. Heart regular, apical murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.
Plan: CMP, lipids, CBC. Fall vaccines: flu, COVID, and RSV this year given his heart failure. LDCT November.

documents.title: Immunizations
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Three vaccines today per PCP: high-dose flu L deltoid, RSV (Abrysvo) R deltoid, 2024-25 Moderna COVID L deltoid lower site. Pressure held on each (on DAPT). Waited 15 minutes, no reaction. Told him a sore arm tomorrow would not be surprising.

Exam: vitals as charted. Heart regular, apical systolic murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.
A/P: HFrEF stable. CAD, no angina. Neuropathic hand pain controlled on gabapentin. BMP. Continue meds; see in spring.

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED.
69-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy, HFrEF and anterior LV aneurysm after an old MI. For two weeks breathlessness has crept up: a flight of stairs or a short walk now stops him. Wakes at night gasping and has gone to three pillows. No chest pain, fever or recent illness.
Vitals: T 36.9, BP 102/66, HR 108, RR 24, SpO2 89% on room air.
Exam: mildly distressed, using accessory muscles. Late inspiratory crackles at both bases, no wheeze. S3 gallop. Mild pitting edema both legs.
CXR: bilateral perihilar opacities, pulmonary edema. NT-proBNP 4850. Troponin not elevated.
Plan: oxygen, IV furosemide, admit to the cardiac unit. NKDA.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
Admitted 2/26/2025, discharged 3/3/2025.
Diagnosis: acute decompensated heart failure, HFrEF, ischemic cardiomyopathy with anterior LV aneurysm.
Course: hypoxic with pulmonary edema on arrival. A pulmonary artery catheter was placed in the cardiac unit on the first night to guide therapy given soft blood pressure; wedge pressure elevated at 27 mmHg. IV furosemide with good response, oxygen weaned by day 3, catheter removed day 3. Echo: LVEF 30%, aneurysm unchanged, moderate functional MR. Troponin not elevated, no ischemic trigger found. Weight down 5 kg at discharge. Renal function stable.
Discharge medications (unchanged from home): aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40 daily, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40, gabapentin 300 TID, indomethacin as needed, NTG SL as needed.
NKDA.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week, cardiology 2-3 weeks. Daily weights, 2 g sodium diet, fluid around 2 L.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
First heart failure admission, 2/26 to 3/3, pulmonary edema, diuresed, PA catheter, EF now 30%. Home 3 days. Breathing much better, back to one pillow, can do the porch steps. Weighing daily, holding at discharge weight. Discharge meds reviewed line by line with his pill box: unchanged from before.
Exam: vitals as charted. No JVD. Heart regular, apical systolic murmur, no gallop today. Faint crackles right base. Trace ankle edema.
A/P: HFrEF after decompensation, near dry weight. Continue furosemide 40 daily; extra dose only on instruction. Low-salt diet reviewed. BMP today. Cardiology 3/20.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Cardiology Follow-up
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Seen after his first heart failure hospitalization (late February). Now euvolemic, class II, weight stable at home. LVEF 30% on the inpatient echo with the known anterior aneurysm.
Medications unchanged: aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40, gabapentin, indomethacin as needed, NTG SL as needed. NKDA.
Plan: continue current regimen. Sodium and fluid guidance reinforced. Return in 6 months.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV, 70 last month. Since the February admission he has kept to light jobs. Stairs with mild breathlessness. One pillow. Weights steady. Hands burn mildly; gabapentin continues. Shoulders and elbows ache after work.
Mood screen PHQ-9 4. No falls. Lives alone; brother nearby.
Exam: vitals as charted. Heart regular, murmur unchanged. Lungs clear. No edema.
Plan: CMP, lipids, CBC. Flu and COVID in the fall. LDCT in November. Colonoscopy due 2027. Cardiology in September.

documents.body:
Regional hospital ED.
70M with HFrEF and an anterior LV aneurysm from a prior anterior MI years ago, admitted here in February for decompensated heart failure. Over the last several days, breathlessness has steadily worsened; he wakes up gasping and sleeps propped up on several pillows. Appetite down, legs a little swollen. No chest pain, cough or fever.
Exam: tired, short of breath at rest. S3. Crackles at both bases, no wheeze. JVP elevated. Peripheral pulses weak.
CXR: increased vascular markings, small bilateral effusions. NT-proBNP 6120, troponin not elevated.
Impression: acute pulmonary edema from left heart failure.
Plan: IV diuresis, admit to the cardiac unit; pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring. NKDA.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist

Admitted 9/4/2025, discharged 9/9/2025.
Diagnosis: acute pulmonary edema due to left heart failure; HFrEF (LVEF 30% 2/2025), ischemic cardiomyopathy with anterior aneurysm.
Course: pulmonary artery catheter placed in the cardiac unit for hemodynamic monitoring; PCWP 25 mmHg on placement. IV furosemide, brisk diuresis, catheter out on day 2, off oxygen day 3. Renal function stable. Weight down about 4 kg.
Discharge medications unchanged from home: aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40, gabapentin 300 TID, indomethacin 25 as needed, NTG SL as needed.
NKDA.

Exam: vitals as charted. No JVD. Heart regular, apical murmur, no S3 today. Lungs clear. Trace edema.
A/P: pulmonary edema resolved; HFrEF back to dry weight. Low-sodium cooking reviewed again; he will keep a weight log on the fridge. BMP today. Cardiology in October. Flu and COVID at that time too.

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED.
CC: tired, lightheaded, black stools.
HPI: 70-year-old man with coronary disease (LAD stent), HFrEF with an anterior aneurysm, and a duodenal ulcer years ago, with two weeks of worsening fatigue and lightheadedness when he gets up from a chair. Winded on stairs, more than his usual. Stools black and sticky, which he calls tarry. Some nausea, eating less. No vomiting, no belly pain, no red blood. No fevers, chills or weight loss. He figured he was just getting old and the arthritis was slowing him down. Pulmonary edema admission in September.
Meds: he fills his own pill box and has not gone over it with anyone recently. Takes aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40, gabapentin 300 TID, and indomethacin 25 for joint pain most days lately. NKDA.
Exam: BP 108/66, HR 98, RR 16. Pale and tired. Heart and lungs unremarkable. Abdomen: mild epigastric tenderness, no rebound or guarding, no masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, no signs of chronic liver disease. Rectal: black tarry stool, guaiac positive.
Labs: Hgb 8.2, MCV 82, BUN 38, Cr 1.1, platelets 240,000, INR 1.0.
Impression: upper GI bleed, likely peptic ulcer on NSAID plus dual antiplatelet therapy.
Plan: two large-bore IVs, IV pantoprazole, hold clopidogrel and indomethacin, GI consulted, admit to medicine.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
Admitted 2/19/2026, discharged 2/23/2026.
Diagnosis: bleeding duodenal ulcer, NSAID-associated, on dual antiplatelet therapy. Blood loss anemia.
Course: Hgb 8.2 on arrival with CAD; 1 unit packed red cells given. IV pantoprazole. EGD 2/20: 12 mm duodenal bulb ulcer with a nonbleeding visible vessel, treated with epinephrine injection and two clips. Gastric biopsies negative for H. pylori. No rebleeding. Aspirin 81 continued. Cardiology consulted: more than three years from the LAD stent, stop clopidogrel and continue aspirin alone. Volume status watched closely given HFrEF; home furosemide continued. Hgb 9.1 on day of discharge.
Discharge medications:
- STOP indomethacin. No NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin, etc.).
- STOP clopidogrel.
- pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, then once daily.
- ferrous sulfate 325 mg every other day (new).
- acetaminophen 500 mg 1-2 tablets every 8 hours as needed for joint pain, max 3 g/day (new).
- Continue aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, gabapentin 300 TID, NTG SL as needed.
NKDA.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with CBC; cardiology in 4 weeks.

documents.title: Admission notice
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Hospital notification: Mr. Babcock admitted 2/19 with GI bleed, scoped today. Called his cell; he sounds tired but fine, says the scope found an ulcer and they clipped it. Brother is driving him home when discharged. Post-hospital slot held for 2/26.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Admitted 2/19 to 2/23 for a bleeding duodenal ulcer; EGD with clips, 1 unit of blood, H. pylori negative. Indomethacin and clopidogrel stopped. No black stools since discharge; stools dark green on iron. Less lightheaded. Still tires easily. Breathing at baseline, weight steady.
We went through the bottle bag: indomethacin bottle taken home for disposal by us. He did not realize it could cause a bleed with his other pills.
Exam: vitals as charted. Mild pallor. Heart regular, apical murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No edema.
Labs today: Hgb 9.8, up from 9.1 at discharge.
A/P: bleeding duodenal ulcer, recovering. Pantoprazole 40 BID through about 4/20, then daily. Iron every other day. Aspirin alone. Acetaminophen for joints; no NSAIDs, flagged on his chart. Recheck CBC and ferritin in April. Cardiology 3/19.

documents.title: Stool color
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Stools are still dark, kind of greenish black. Not sticky like before. Is this the iron or should I worry

documents.title: RE: Stool color
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Good question. Iron commonly turns stool dark green to black, and formed stool that isn't sticky or tar-like fits the iron. If it turns tarry again, or you feel faint, short of breath or your heart races, call us right away or go to the ER. Otherwise keep going with the iron and pantoprazole.

documents.title: Cardiology Follow-up
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Letter to PCP. Seen after admission for a bleeding duodenal ulcer while on aspirin, clopidogrel and indomethacin. More than three years from the proximal LAD stent and angina-free; we stopped clopidogrel in hospital and he will remain on aspirin 81 mg alone going forward. Heart failure stable, class II, euvolemic.
Medications: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, furosemide 40, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40 BID (to daily after 8 weeks), ferrous sulfate, gabapentin, acetaminophen as needed, NTG SL as needed. NKDA. No NSAIDs.
Return in 6 months.

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Eight weeks since the ulcer bleed. Energy much better, back to half days of work. No melena, no abdominal pain. Taking iron every other day without trouble. Joints manageable on acetaminophen, though he grumbles that it is not as good as the indomethacin was.
Exam: color better. Heart regular. Abdomen soft, nontender.
Labs today: Hgb 11.6, ferritin 18, iron 48, saturation 13%.
A/P: bleeding duodenal ulcer, healing course. Pantoprazole down to 40 daily today and continued while on aspirin. Iron stores still low: continue ferrous sulfate. CBC again at the June AWV.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV, 71 last month. Good spring. No black stools since February. Energy close to normal. Heart failure: one flight with a pause, unchanged; one pillow; weights steady. No angina. Hands burn on and off, gabapentin continues. Shoulders and elbows ache on work days; acetaminophen takes the edge off.
Medication review done together with his pill box, now 10 items; NSAID avoidance reviewed again.
PHQ-2 1. No falls. Lives alone, brother nearby, proxy unchanged.
Exam: vitals as charted. Heart regular, apical murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.
Labs: Hgb 12.9.
A/P: bleeding duodenal ulcer resolved; history kept on the list. Continue pantoprazole daily, iron for now, aspirin alone. CMP, lipids today. CBC in August. Flu and COVID in the fall. LDCT November. Colonoscopy due 2027.
